newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST-US industrial output seen up again in Dec.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-US industrial output seen up again in Dec.

text.p: Lean inventories and rising demand for exports probably boosted U.S. industrial production last month, suggesting strong manufacturing momentum into early 1997, economists said on Wednesday.
"Manufacturing, especially ex-autos, is booming," said Jim O'Sullivan, an economist at J.P. Morgan & Co.
The Federal Reserve will release its report on December industrial production on Friday at 0830 EST/1330 GMT.
Wall Street analysts estimated industrial output rose 0.6 percent in December after a 0.9 percent increase in November.
They forecast that capacity utilization climbed to 83.5 percent from 83.3 percent.

"I think the interesting question right now is, why is manufacturing starting to accelerate again," O'Sullivan said. "We suspect exports are picking up here and that's really driving manufacturing stronger."
The pace of global growth quickened over the past year, swelling international demand for U.S. products despite a stronger dollar, O'Sullivan said.

Dan Seto, senior economist at Nikko Securities Co International Inc, said lean inventories in November led to production growth in December. Business inventories, for example, rose 0.1 percent in November, compared with a 0.5 percent increase the month before.
Friday's report will fuel further speculation about a Fed rate hike sometime in the first quarter, analysts said.
"This probably will add to fears of a Fed tightening, but I don't think they'll do it in early February," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc.
An industrial production figure near the 0.6 percent consensus would be consistent with speedy Gross Domestic Product growth of about 3.5 percent in the fourth quarter of 1996, the economists said.
The central bank is widely believed to perceive 2.0 to 2.5 percent as the nation's long-term non-inflationary potential growth rate.
The capacity utilization number might be more troubling to the Fed since the series has a historical correlation with inflation, some economists said.
"Large inflation waves seem to have coincided not only with high capacity use but also energy price problems," said Nikko's Seto. "We're kind of encountering a mini-cycle of that right now."
Recently, however, inflation upticks generally have been limited to energy prices and wages, so capacity utilization may not have reached stressful levels, Seto said.
"We've seen capacity use up in this region (around 83.0 percent) for some time now, and that really has not generated inflation yet," he said.
Looking ahead, economists called for healthy industrial production for the next several months. Output probably will fall off, but it will be falling from relatively high levels, they said.
"This is consistent with a lot of the other data we've been seeing lately, which is that the economy has some momentum behind it again," said O'Sullivan.
